title: U.S. Measles Cases Nearly Match 35-Year Record With Five Months Left in 2026
excerpt: The CDC has confirmed 2,231 measles cases through early July, just 58 short of last year's full-year total that was the highest since 1991. Health experts say the record will fall well before year's end.
body:
• The CDC confirmed 2,231 measles cases in 2026 as of July 9, nearly matching 2025's full-year total of 2,289 — the highest since 1991.
  • Ninety-two percent of cases occurred in unvaccinated individuals, and 72% were in children aged 19 and younger.
  • The Pan American Health Organization will review in November whether the U.S. has lost its measles elimination status, held since 2000.
  • Outbreaks are active across 41 jurisdictions, with South Carolina, Utah, Texas, Virginia, and Arizona hardest hit.

The United States is on the verge of setting a grim public health milestone. As of July 9, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has confirmed 2,231 measles cases in 2026 — just 58 fewer than the 2,289 cases recorded for all of 2025, which was itself the highest annual total in 35 years, according to USA Today and CDC data.

With five months of the year remaining — including summer travel season and the back-to-school period that historically drives transmission spikes — public health experts say surpassing the record is all but certain.

"This year, we've seen an even sharper increase in measles cases. If this trend continues, we will easily surpass the 2025 number of cases."

— Dr. William Moss, Executive Director, International Vaccine Access Center, Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health

A Resurgence Driven by Declining Vaccination

The surge traces back to outbreaks that began in 2025 and have continued into this year. Of the 2,170 cases tallied by the CDC through early July, 93% were linked to 31 identified outbreaks. Some 1,360 of those cases stem from outbreaks that originated in 2025 and never stopped, while 659 are tied to 31 new outbreaks in 2026, according to the CDC's July 2 data update reported by Medical Daily.

The pattern is overwhelmingly concentrated among the unvaccinated. Ninety-two percent of this year's cases have occurred in people who were either unvaccinated or had unknown vaccination status. Just 4% had received one dose of the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine, and another 4% had received two doses, according to the CDC.

Children bear a disproportionate burden. More than half of all cases — 52% — have occurred in children and adolescents aged 5 to 19, and another 21% in children under 5, according to Healio. At least 127 hospitalizations have been recorded, and three deaths have been confirmed across the 2025–2026 outbreak period — two unvaccinated children in Texas and one adult in New Mexico.

Hardest-Hit States and Spreading Outbreaks

The largest case concentrations remain in states where outbreaks have persisted since last year. South Carolina leads with 670 confirmed cases, followed by Utah with 516, Texas with 182, and Virginia with 177, according to CDC data cited by USA Today. Arizona's count has reached 117, with Maricopa County alone reporting 25 cases — up from its 30-year average of one per year, county health officials said on July 17.

https://x.com/ScienceAlert/status/2079692767140425857

The outbreak is no longer confined to predictable pockets. Cases have now been reported in 41 jurisdictions across the country. California has recorded 51 cases as of July 6, including infections in the Bay Area's Santa Clara and San Francisco counties, according to the California Department of Public Health. In the mid-Atlantic region, Maryland tripled its 2025 case count after five new cases were confirmed on July 16 in residents who had traveled to an area with an active outbreak.

Elimination Status at Stake

The stakes extend beyond case counts. A Washington Post investigation published in early July identified two structural factors making the 2026 surge harder to contain than previous outbreaks: unvaccinated communities that are now larger, more interconnected, and harder to isolate; and a hollowed-out public health workforce weakened by post-pandemic budget cuts and attrition, according to a Medical Daily analysis of the investigation.

The Pan American Health Organization is scheduled to review in November whether the United States still qualifies for measles elimination status — a designation it has held since 2000. Whole-genome sequencing of the D8-9171 measles lineage shows it has circulated continuously since January 2025, evidence that public health experts at Johns Hopkins and the University of Minnesota's CIDRAP say is consistent with sustained domestic transmission.

"The high number of U.S. measles cases is concerning and threatens the U.S. measles elimination status."

— Dr. Yvonne "Bonnie" A. Maldonado, Professor of Global Health and Infectious Diseases, Stanford University School of Medicine

What It Means for the Indian Diaspora

The resurgence carries particular relevance for Indian Americans, many of whom travel frequently between the U.S. and South Asia. India has faced its own measles challenges in recent years, and neighboring Bangladesh is currently experiencing a devastating outbreak — with nearly 800 deaths and over 119,000 suspected cases reported as of late July, according to Bangladesh's Directorate General of Health Services. Bay Area counties with significant South Asian populations, including Santa Clara and San Francisco, have recorded cases this year, and local health officers have urged residents — particularly those planning international travel — to verify their MMR vaccination status.

What to Watch

The CDC continues to publish weekly case updates, and the trajectory suggests the 2025 record will be surpassed within weeks. The PAHO review in November will determine whether the U.S. officially loses its elimination status — a decision hinging on whether genomic evidence confirms continuous domestic transmission for more than 12 months. With school reopenings approaching in August and September, public health officials are urging families to confirm their children have received two doses of the MMR vaccine, which provides 97% protection against measles.
